abstract: Quantum reservoir computing processes time series by injecting one input per time step into a fixed, noisy quantum system and training only a linear readout. A reservoir can solve a temporal task only if the inputs the task needs are still present in its state. What fundamentally limits this memory? Adding qubits seems the natural way to extend it. However, noise injects entropy into every qubit at every time step, and under depolarizing noise a reservoir can remove this entropy steadily only through the input qubits that are reinitialized at each time step. Here we show that this number, not the size of the reservoir, sets the memory. With k reinitialized input qubits per time step, the largest attainable memory depth at fixed accuracy is exp[Θ(k)] time steps once the initial state has been washed out, independent of the total number of qubits. The upper bound holds for every reservoir unitary and input encoding, and an explicit construction shows that the exponential scaling is attainable. Retaining an input for T time steps therefore requires Θ(log T) reinitialized input qubits per time step. Unital noise leaves this limit unchanged, whereas non-unital noise acts as an additional entropy sink. These results identify reinitialized input qubits, not reservoir size, as the fundamental resource for memory in quantum reservoir computing, and make memory a quantity that can be budgeted in the design of quantum reservoirs.

justification: We identify a resource law for memory in noisy quantum dynamics. At fixed accuracy and independent depolarizing noise, the greatest attainable memory depth grows exponentially with the number of qubits reinitialized per step, independently of reservoir size after initialization decays. A uniform upper bound and an explicit construction establish both sides of this scaling. Additional unital noise preserves the bound, while cooling supplies another entropy sink. This connects quantum information retention, open system dynamics, and physical computing through a shared resource accounting. We believe this perspective can interest physicists beyond reservoir computing and guide the design of driven quantum devices.
